title: Hailey Baptiste stuns Aryna Sabalenka, saving six match points in Madrid Open nail-biter
content:
MADRID — Aryna Sabalenka finally lost a tennis match. Hailey Baptiste took it from her.

Sabalenka, the world No. 1, had won 15 consecutive matches across three tournaments and looked on her way to her 16th until Baptiste, the quickly-improving American with a smooth all-court game and a dangerous mix of power and spin, caught fire in the second set of their Madrid Open quarterfinal Tuesday night.

Baptiste barely missed long stretches, carried the momentum into the third set and outlasted Sabalenka down the stretch in a nail-biting sequence of games and then a tiebreak for a 2-6, 6-2, 7-6(6) win. Baptiste saved six match points, inflicting Sabalenka’s first defeat having held even one since the 2024 Madrid Open.

“It just shows me where my game was. I’ve always believed it, and I feel like now I’m starting to put it into action and the world is seeing it as well,” Baptiste told Tennis Channel when it was over.

The American appeared to confuse Sabalenka with the combination of her slice backhand and whipping forehand. For a good while, Sabalenka spent as much time twisting her neck to watch balls whizz past her as she did setting up winners of her own.

Sabalenka has been mostly flawless this year. She was 26-1 coming into the match against Baptiste. Her lone blemish was a loss in the final of the Australian Open, where Elena Rybakina beat her 6-4, 4-6, 6-4.

Baptiste appeared to get the decisive break in the seventh game of the third set, unleashing a series of heavy, topspin forehands that darted into the clay just ahead of the baseline. They were the kind of balls that Sabalenka has tortured opponents with all season.

But Sabalenka broke right black, blasting a crosscourt backhand to even the score at 4-4. Sabalenka held serve and had four match points with Baptiste serving at 4-5. Baptiste smacked an ace to save the first one and cracked an inside-out forehand to save the second. Baptiste serve-and-volleyed on her second serve to save the third. Then she did it again on the fourth, inducing a wide backhand from Sabalenka. On the fifth, a drop shot and lob volley combination got Baptiste out of trouble.

Two points later, she zipped a backhand down the line to knot the set at 5-5 and put the pressure squarely onto the other side of the court. From there, Baptiste played free once more. She attacked Sabalenka’s serve. She cracked a forehand winner down the line and got the break when Sabalenka sent a forehand several feet off the court.

Now she needed to close out the world No. 1. Sabalenka helped her by netting an easy chance at a backhand put-away. But then Sabalenka found the court on a couple of big returns and off they went to a tiebreak.

Advantage Sabalenka, the best tiebreak player in the sport. At 4-3, she hit a nifty drop volley from inches above the clay to move two points from the match. But Baptiste went on the attack and drew even at 5-5.

A forehand long gave Sabalenka a sixth match point, this one on her serve. She missed a backhand down the line by inches, then hit a forehand into the net to give Baptiste her first match point.

That was all she needed. A crosscourt forehand to the postage stamp finished it. She spread her arms, allowed a brief smile, the kind that had crossed her face when she was double-faulting and having to dig deep late in the third set, and made her way to the net for a handshake and a hug.

“I definitely had a lot of nerves, but I had 28 chances yesterday and I didn’t get it done,” she said.

“I was able to get it on the first one, and I told my team, when I get my match point today, I’m going to win the first one that I get.”

Sabalenka had gone to three sets three times during her 15-match win streak, most recently on Monday against Naomi Osaka. Each time she had found her way out of trouble. She looked like she was going to this time, too. Instead, trouble and Baptiste found her.

On Monday, after her win over Osaka, Sabalenka said her hatred of losing has helped motivate her to win so much. “The worst feeling for an athlete,” she said.

Tuesday night she took her bag, marched off the court, grabbed her puppy, Ashe, and headed into the news conference room.

“He’s my emotional support,” she said as she cradled her cavalier King Charles spaniel.

“I had some opportunities in the third set, and I felt like I was maybe a little bit rushing the point,” she said. “Sometimes I guess you have to learn. Take the best from this week and move on.”

“She played really brave tennis,” Sabalenka said of Baptiste.

They had met as recently as March at the Miami Open, also in a quarterfinal. Sabalenka said she didn’t give Baptiste opportunities there.

“Here, the first game, second set, I just double-faulted twice out of nowhere, and I felt like that gave her belief,” she said. “After that, she just started playing more aggressively. As I said, she was playing great tennis. What can I say, well done.”

Baptiste, a product of the Junior Tennis Champions Center, the Maryland training ground that produced her close friend Frances Tiafoe, was struggling to stay in the top 100 a year ago. Tiafoe’s brother, Franklin, became an integral part of her coaching team and was in the box Tuesday night at Manolo Santana Stadium.

Baptiste has spent the past year methodically climbing the rankings. First she began making her way through qualifying rounds. She beat Beatriz Haddad Maia at Roland Garros and made the round of 16. She beat a hot Victoria Mboko at Wimbledon and made the third round. In Miami last month, she beat Elina Svitolins and Jelena Ostapenko to make the quarters, where she fell to Sabalenka. She’d been kind of close, getting broken once in each set.

“I had a better idea of how to play her and how I should play, adjustments I need to make,” she said in her news conference. “I just went in trying to play my game, still doing the same things that I’ve been doing.”

She stuck with that plan through all six match points.

“Play one more point, make one more ball, and make sure that I’m making her earn that point,” she said. “If she was going to win it, she was going to have to earn it. And I knew that she obviously was feeling a little nervous too.”

And she was bold when she needed to be, serving and volleying and going for the big shot when the chance arrived.

“The plan kind of comes to my head when I get to the line sometimes, and that was what my brain was telling me to do, and so that’s what I did, and it worked,” she said. “It doesn’t always work, but in that moment it did.”

Baptiste has also figured out how to stay out of her own way. She lost match points in a second-set tiebreak Monday against Belinda Bencic. She had an epic racket smash, settled herself, then cruised through the third set. Tuesday night she served for the match and got broken, then was down in the tiebreak. She double-faulted. She laughed.

“I just decided, to stop fighting myself, basically,” she said. “It’s just a decision, like either you get over it or you, or you sit in that feeling and sitting in that feeling has gotten me nowhere.”

Doing something else has gotten her into her first WTA 1000 semifinal – and past the world No. 1.
